s: Classifications based on sex must serve important governmental objectives and be substantially related to achieving them (Craig v. Boren, 1976).
United States v. Virginia (1996) required an "exceedingly persuasive justification."
The justification must be genuine, not invented for litigation, and must not rely on overbroad generalizations about men and women.
Frontiero v. Richardson (1973) had a plurality for strict scrutiny but never a majority.
Nonmarital children ("illegitimacy"): classifications must be substantially related to an important interest (Clark v. Jeter, 1988).
United States v. Skrmetti (2025) upheld Tennessee's ban on certain medical treatments for transgender minors under rational-basis review.
The majority characterized the law as classifying by age and medical use, not by sex or transgender status.
The Court did not decide whether transgender status is a quasi-suspect class.
